South Korea has named seven priority critical minerals, including rare earths, and pledged support for overseas mining and refining investments.

editorial.headline: Divided Government Is a Chance to Fix Health Care, Not an Excuse to Stall
body: The midterms handed Democrats both chambers of Congress, and Washington is already settling into its familiar post-election posture: each side declaring a mandate, each side daring the other to blink. Health care is where that reflex would do the most harm. The president says his team is negotiating with lawmakers and has floated sending government money “directly to the people” rather than to insurers. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has publicly invited him to put his name on a streamlined, Medicare-style programme, mock gold “TrumpCare” card and all. Much of this is theatre. But theatre that admits the other side might have a point is a better starting position than either party has had in years.

Both camps should be honest about the trade-offs. Progressives who want universal coverage have to reckon with cost, with the disruption to the roughly half of Americans who get insurance through work and like it, and with a federal budget already strained by a war and high energy prices. Conservatives who want more consumer control and less insurer middleman have to reckon with the fact that cash in hand does not buy coverage for people with chronic illness unless the rules on pre-existing conditions and risk pools hold firm. Price transparency, site-neutral payments, faster generic and biosimilar approvals and a durable fix to premium subsidies are not the whole answer, but they are the part on which credible economists of both left and right broadly agree.

The temptation for a newly empowered Democratic Congress will be to pass maximal bills for the 2028 campaign; the temptation for the White House will be to sign nothing that hands the opposition a win. Voters, who just punished the governing party in large part over the cost of living, deserve better than a two-year standoff. A modest, bipartisan bill that lowers what families actually pay would not settle the larger argument about who should run American health care. It would show that divided government can still deliver, which may be the most valuable thing either side could offer right now.

debates.question: Was Governor Newsom right to commute every death sentence in California?
debates.context: On 5 November Governor Gavin Newsom announced he would commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole, saying the state “cannot morally kill them.” District attorneys from 30 counties and the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation have asked the courts to halt the move, and 382 of the cases, involving prisoners with more than one felony conviction, require approval by at least four of the seven California Supreme Court justices before Newsom leaves office in January. President Trump said this week that the Justice Department is working to overturn the decision.

views.label: Yes
views.headline: A Punishment the State Will Not Carry Out Is Not Justice
body: California has not executed anyone since 2006. Newsom imposed a moratorium in 2019, and long before that, litigation over lethal-injection protocols had frozen the machinery. The result is a death row that functions as an extraordinarily expensive form of life imprisonment, with years of mandatory appeals, separate housing and specialised counsel, while victims’ families are promised a finality that never arrives. Converting those sentences to life without parole does not release anyone. It replaces a fiction with a sentence the state will actually enforce.

The moral case matters too, and Newsom made it plainly. The death penalty is the one punishment that cannot be corrected when the system errs, and the American system does err: more than 190 people sentenced to death nationwide have later been exonerated since the 1970s. California’s death row also reflects the familiar distortions of capital punishment, in which the county where a crime occurred and the quality of a defendant’s lawyer can matter as much as the facts of the case. A governor who believes the state cannot fairly administer irreversible punishment has not only the right but arguably the duty to say so.

Clemency is not a loophole. It is written into the California constitution precisely as a check on the courts and the legislature, and the framers attached a safeguard to it: for repeat felons, the state Supreme Court must concur. That review is happening now. If the justices conclude that individual cases deserve a different outcome, the constitution lets them say so. The process critics call lawless is in fact the process the constitution prescribes.

None of this diminishes the suffering of victims’ families, and Newsom was right to acknowledge that the announcement could reopen wounds. The state should have done far better at notifying them, and should invest in the services, restitution and support that matter to survivors long after the headlines fade. But decades of unfulfilled promises have not served those families either. An honest sentence of life behind bars, with no further rounds of appeals and hearings, may offer them more peace than a death sentence that exists only on paper.

views.label: No
views.headline: One Governor Should Not Erase Hundreds of Verdicts at Once
body: Every one of the 548 sentences Newsom commuted was handed down by a jury, reviewed by judges and, in most cases, upheld on appeal. California voters have repeatedly declined to abolish capital punishment: they rejected repeal measures in 2012 and 2016, and in 2016 approved a measure to speed up executions instead. Whatever one thinks of the death penalty, that is a democratic verdict. A blanket commutation announced two months before a governor leaves office substitutes the conviction of one official for the repeated judgment of the electorate.

Clemency exists to correct injustice in particular cases: a doubtful conviction, an inadequate defence, a prisoner transformed by decades of reflection. That is why it has traditionally been granted case by case. The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation’s lawsuit makes exactly this point, arguing that commuting every sentence without individualised review stretches the power beyond its purpose. Treating the man who murdered several children identically to a defendant with a plausible innocence claim is not mercy. It is a policy change dressed in the language of mercy.

The process has also been hard on the people with the most at stake. Former Sacramento District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert has said victims’ families were not notified in advance, and relatives have described learning the news from the media. Many of those families spent years in courtrooms trusting that the law would mean what it said. Telling them, all at once and after an election, that it will not, is a breach of faith that will make future victims less willing to trust the system.

There is a better path for those who want to end the death penalty in California: persuade voters or the legislature to repeal it, and let the change apply openly and prospectively. The 30 county prosecutors challenging the commutations are not asking for executions tomorrow. They are asking the California Supreme Court to insist that the gravest sentences the state imposes be reconsidered on their individual merits, not swept away by decree. That is a reasonable request, and the court should grant it.

debates.bottom_line: Both sides agree that California’s current system, in which death sentences are imposed but not carried out, serves neither justice nor victims’ families, and that survivors deserved better notice and support. The open question is who should end the impasse: a governor using a constitutional clemency power, or voters and courts weighing each case on its own merits?

debates.question: Should the United States ease its naval blockade of Iran to get formal peace talks started?
debates.context: A US naval blockade has largely choked off Iran’s crude exports since mid-July, and Tehran says it will not reopen formal negotiations or the Strait of Hormuz until the blockade ends, sanctions are eased and frozen assets released. This week President Trump gave Iran until early 2027 to reach a deal, warned that ships trying to breach the blockade would be sunk, and suggested strikes could resume next year if talks fail; Qatar and Pakistan are mediating. Elevated fuel and shipping costs have become a domestic political issue.

views.label: Yes
views.headline: Leverage Is Only Worth Something If You Are Willing to Spend It
body: The blockade has done its job. It has squeezed Iran’s oil revenue for more than four months and demonstrated that Washington can impose real costs without a ground war. But leverage is a means, not an end. A blockade that continues indefinitely, with no diplomatic process attached, turns from pressure into a standoff, and standoffs at sea have a way of ending in accidents. When the president is warning that ships will be sunk and Iran is vowing to break the cordon, the risk of an incident that drags both sides back into open war is not hypothetical.

The costs are not borne only by Tehran. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has kept shipping and fuel costs high, and that has hit American households and US allies in Europe and Asia. Voters just registered their frustration with the cost of living at the ballot box. A carefully sequenced easing of the blockade, tied to verifiable steps such as safe passage through the strait and a return to the table, would ease that pain while keeping most of Washington’s pressure, including sanctions, in place.

Easing is not the same as surrender. The United States could offer a partial, reversible step, such as allowing limited humanitarian or civilian shipping, in exchange for Iran beginning formal talks through the Qatari and Pakistani channels and halting drone launches. If Tehran stalls, the cordon can be restored within days; the Navy is not going anywhere. That is a far smaller gamble than letting the deadline approach with no process at all and then facing a choice between climbing down and resuming strikes.

History counsels humility about maximalist goals in this region. Trump’s own talk of “total victory” sits awkwardly with his statement that the war is effectively over militarily. If the military phase is done, the task now is to convert battlefield gains into a durable settlement on Iran’s nuclear programme and on freedom of navigation. That requires talks, and talks require a reason for the other side to come. A measured, conditional gesture is the cheapest way to provide one.

views.label: No
views.headline: Lifting the Pressure First Would Reward the Tactic That Started This
body: Iran’s position is straightforward: end the blockade, waive oil sanctions and release frozen funds, and only then will it talk seriously. Accepting those terms would mean paying the full price of a deal before negotiations begin. That is not diplomacy; it is ransom. The leverage that brought Tehran to indirect contact through Qatar and Pakistan is the blockade itself, and giving it away up front would leave Washington with little to trade when the hard questions about uranium enrichment and missile programmes finally arrive.

The record of this conflict argues for caution. An April ceasefire collapsed within two weeks after attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and a later memorandum proved no more durable. Each pause gave Iran room to regroup. The president said this week that Iran has launched more drones and missiles in the past week than at any time in over a year. That is not the behaviour of a government preparing to bargain in good faith, and it is not the moment to signal that pressure will lift if Tehran simply waits.

The economic argument for easing is weaker than it looks. Oil has kept moving through the strait with US military assistance, while Iran’s own exports remain choked off. Analysts have noted that this asymmetry steadily erodes Iran’s bargaining power over time. High fuel prices are painful, but a premature deal that leaves Iran free to threaten the world’s most important energy chokepoint again would impose far larger costs on consumers in the years ahead.

None of this means ruling out a settlement. The administration has set a clear window, through early 2027, and kept channels open through two credible mediators. The right sequence is for Iran to take concrete steps first, such as halting attacks on shipping and agreeing to formal talks, with relief on the blockade offered in return for verifiable commitments. Firmness now is what makes a lasting agreement possible later.

debates.bottom_line: Both sides want an end to the war that secures shipping through Hormuz and constrains Iran’s nuclear programme, and both accept that some sequencing of blockade relief and Iranian concessions will eventually be needed. The open question is who moves first: does a conditional easing now lower the risk of a wider war, or does it squander the leverage that makes a durable deal possible?

debates.question: Was Nvidia’s board right to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive?
debates.context: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after reports of an extramarital relationship, with one woman tied in reports to suspected Chinese espionage; on 17 November the board said it did not intend to reinstate him and hired a search firm. On 23 November the board voted unanimously to bring him back, saying it had received input from senior US government officials, while an independent committee continues its investigation. Shares jumped sharply, but governance experts and some large investors have questioned the board’s independence, and a congressional interview with Huang is scheduled for 1 December.

views.label: Yes
views.headline: The Board’s Duty Is to Shareholders, and Shareholders Voted With Their Feet
body: Few companies are as identified with a single leader as Nvidia is with Jensen Huang, who co-founded it in 1993 and steered it from a graphics-card maker into the central supplier of the AI era. Boards owe their duty to shareholders, and the market’s verdict on his return was immediate: the stock rose sharply on the announcement. Directors who ignored that signal, and the operational risk of a leaderless company in the middle of an intense global race for AI chips, would have been failing at their core job.

Reinstatement is not exoneration, and the board has not pretended otherwise. Its filing says a committee of independent directors will carry the investigation to its conclusion, that Colette Kress returns to her role as finance chief, and that the company will search for a new chief compliance officer. Those are serious structural commitments. If the investigation turns up wrongdoing, the board retains every power to act. Bringing Huang back while it finishes is a judgement about who is best placed to run the business in the meantime, not a verdict on the facts.

The national-security dimension cuts in favour of continuity, not against it. Nvidia’s chips sit at the heart of US export-control policy and America’s technological contest with China. If senior government officials concluded that stable leadership at Nvidia serves the national interest, the board was right to weigh that view, especially when Huang has agreed to sit for questioning by congressional committees. A drawn-out succession fight would have handed competitors and adversaries an opening.

Corporate governance is supposed to protect owners, not to satisfy abstract standards at their expense. The board made a hard call quickly, reversed itself when it received new information, and attached safeguards to the decision. That is not a failure of independence. It is what a board does when it takes both its oversight role and its fiduciary duty seriously.

views.label: No
views.headline: A Board That Reverses Itself Under Political Pressure Has a Problem
body: Six days after telling investors it did not intend to reinstate Huang, Nvidia’s board did exactly that, before its own investigation had concluded. New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who oversees pension money invested in the company, has said directors reversed course without explanation. Governance experts quoted by Reuters made the same point: the purpose of an independent investigation is to establish the facts before deciding who leads the company, not after.

The most troubling detail is the board’s own acknowledgement that it received input from senior US government officials, alongside reports that the president urged the move and the vice president worked with directors on it. Whatever one thinks of the outcome, the precedent is corrosive. Shareholders, not the White House, own Nvidia. If the government can shape the leadership of the world’s most valuable chipmaker by phone call, every board of a strategically important company will now have to wonder whose interests it is really serving.

The underlying questions are not trivial. California’s Justice Department is examining whether Nvidia chips or confidential information may have reached China and whether investors were misled, and congressional committees want to hear from Huang. Those inquiries go to the heart of the company’s compliance with export controls that underpin US national security. Restoring the chief executive before they are resolved suggests that the outcome was settled in advance, which undercuts the credibility of the very investigation the board says it is continuing.

A share-price jump is not a governance argument. Markets reward short-term certainty, but they also punish companies when hidden risks surface later, and boards exist precisely to take the longer view. The better course would have been an interim leadership team, a swift and transparent investigation, and a decision on Huang’s future once the facts were in. Nvidia’s shareholders, and the country that depends on its chips, deserved that patience.

debates.bottom_line: Both sides agree that Huang has been central to Nvidia’s success, that the investigation into his conduct and any China-related risks must be completed rigorously, and that the company’s chips matter to US national security. The open question is how much weight a board should give to market reaction and government input when deciding who leads a company before the facts are fully known.

debates.question: Should states pause new AI data center construction until rules on power costs are in place?
debates.context: Data centers and electricity prices became a major issue in this month’s midterms, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress; voters in about a dozen states backed ballot measures restricting data centers, and more than 100 moratoriums have been proposed at various levels of government. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a national moratorium, while most federal lawmakers, Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs and a range of analysts oppose one, arguing instead for making data centers pay their own grid costs.

views.label: Yes
views.headline: Hit Pause Until the Rules Protect Ratepayers
body: Voters have spoken with unusual clarity. Data centers were one of the defining local issues of the midterms, ballot measures restricting them passed across roughly a dozen states, and polling shows large majorities would oppose a new facility in their own area, with rising electricity prices the leading reason. When a technology that promises enormous benefits generates that much grassroots resistance, the problem is not public ignorance. It is that the rules governing who pays for the grid were written for a different era.

A data center campus can demand as much power as a small city, and the transmission lines, substations and generation built to serve it are typically financed through rates that every customer pays. Companies have offered voluntary pledges, and the White House introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March, but voluntary commitments are not enforceable tariffs. A time-limited pause, such as the moratorium Maine has moved toward, gives regulators breathing room to write binding rules: large loads pay the full cost of the infrastructure they require, and projects bring their own new generation rather than drawing down existing capacity.

A pause is also about more than electricity. Communities have legitimate questions about water use, noise, land and the modest number of permanent jobs these facilities create relative to their footprint and tax incentives. Pausing new approvals for a defined period, while letting projects already under construction proceed, is a measured way to answer those questions before commitments are locked in for decades.

Nothing here is anti-technology. America should lead in artificial intelligence. But public consent is a resource too, and it is being spent fast. A short, rules-focused pause now is far more likely to secure a durable licence for AI infrastructure than pressing ahead and inviting the outright bans that some communities, such as Monterey Park in California, have already chosen.

views.label: No
views.headline: Fix the Tariffs, Not the Construction Schedule
body: The intuition that data centers are driving up household power bills is understandable but incomplete. Analysts at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation note that retail electricity prices track fuel costs, especially natural gas, far more closely than any single source of demand. A City Journal analysis of Berkeley Lab data found that inflation-adjusted residential electricity prices actually fell in 23 states between 2019 and 2025. Where bills have risen, policy choices about transmission, generation and rate design are usually the bigger culprits.

A moratorium would not even address the problem it targets. Projects already approved and under construction would still come online and still draw power. What a pause would do is freeze new investment, push it to other states or countries, and raise the cost of the computing capacity on which American competitiveness in AI increasingly depends. That is why most federal lawmakers have rejected the idea, and why a Democratic governor in Arizona, Katie Hobbs, has also declined to impose one.

The better answer is already emerging across party lines: make large loads pay their own way. Regulators can require data centers to fund the grid upgrades they trigger, sign long-term contracts that protect other ratepayers if demand falls short, and bring new generation, from gas to nuclear to renewables plus storage, onto the grid. Turning voluntary pledges into enforceable tariff rules would address the legitimate fairness concern without halting construction.

Data centers also bring real benefits to the communities that host them: property-tax revenue that funds schools and services, construction work, and large private investment in grid capacity that can strengthen reliability for everyone if planned well. States that write clear rules will capture those benefits; states that simply say no will watch them go elsewhere. The goal should be abundant, affordable power for households and industry alike, not scarcity managed by moratorium.

debates.bottom_line: Both sides agree that households should not be left paying for grid upgrades that serve large data centers, and that voluntary corporate pledges are not enough. The open question is sequencing: is a temporary pause the only way to get binding cost-allocation rules written, or can regulators impose those rules while construction continues?

pieces.headline: Held Up by Silicon: How the AI Building Boom Is Masking an Oil Shock and a Debt Problem
pieces.dek: Global growth has survived the largest energy disruption on record largely because a handful of companies are pouring concrete and chips into data centres, a support that is real, concentrated and increasingly debt-financed.
key_findings: The IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects global growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, and attributes its slight upgrade largely to continued AI infrastructure investment.

The OECD is more cautious, putting 2026 growth at 2.9% and 2027 at 3.0% in its September interim outlook, and estimating that combined downside risks could cut growth by 0.7 percentage points and add 1.1 points to inflation.
Big Tech capital spending plans for 2026 are estimated at roughly $650-800bn across the four largest US hyperscalers, with one tally putting it at $725bn, up 77% on 2025.
The BIS warns that a rising share of AI capex is debt-financed, including off-balance-sheet 'shadow borrowing' through special-purpose vehicles held by private credit funds and insurers.
Global public debt stood at just under 94% of GDP in 2025 and the IMF projects it will reach 100% by around the end of the decade, limiting governments' room to cushion any reversal.
body: On paper, 2026 should have been a recession year. The disruption to flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which the International Energy Agency now calls the largest energy supply shock the world has faced, pushed oil above $100 a barrel for much of the year. Yet the world's two main macroeconomic forecasters ended the autumn with growth projections close to 3%. The IMF's October World Economic Outlook, titled 'Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices', puts global growth at 3.1% this year and 3.4% in 2027. The OECD's September interim report has 2.9% and 3.0%, a touch better than the 2.8% it pencilled in for 2026 in June.

The explanation both institutions reach for is the same: investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The IMF said its small upgrade was largely due to continued strong spending on data centres, chips and the power to run them. The scale is unusual for any single category of private investment. Estimates of 2026 capital expenditure by Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta compiled from mid-year earnings range from about $650bn to $800bn; one widely cited tally put it at $725bn, a 77% rise on a record $410bn in 2025. Company guidance has repeatedly been revised up: Microsoft has pointed to around $190bn for calendar 2026, Alphabet to $180-190bn earlier in the year, Meta to $125-145bn, and Amazon to somewhere between $200bn and $220bn depending on the source and date.

There are good reasons to be cautious about reading this as broad-based strength. First, the boost is geographically narrow. The IMF expects US growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, and notes that the AI lift to US output is partly offset by the large import content of servers and components, meaning that some of the demand leaks to chip and hardware producers in Asia. Second, the boom is itself inflationary at the margin. The IMF projects global headline inflation of 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, and says AI investment adds upward pressure on prices, on top of the energy shock. Microsoft's own guidance attributed about $25bn of its 2026 spending to higher component prices rather than extra capacity.

Third, the financing is changing character. In its January bulletin and a March Quarterly Review box, the Bank for International Settlements documented how hyperscaler spending has outgrown internal cash flow, so that a rising share is borrowed. Corporate bonds remain the main channel, but the BIS highlights joint ventures and special-purpose vehicles that raise debt via private placements, serviced by lease payments from the tech companies and held by private credit funds and insurers. It describes these as 'shadow borrowing' and flags new transmission channels: refinancing pressure at vehicle level, procyclical swings in private credit appetite, and bank credit lines to the vehicles. Credit default swap spreads widened during the year, especially for lower-rated hyperscalers.

The bullish reading is that this is productive capital deepening, analogous to railways or fibre, financed by some of the most profitable companies in history, and that the IMF itself lists more persistent AI investment as an upside risk. Markets have been discriminating rather than indiscriminate: according to earnings-season coverage, firms that tied capex to visible demand were rewarded while those that raised guidance without a clear monetisation story were sold off. On this view, the energy shock was absorbed because the world economy had a genuine new source of demand at exactly the right moment.

The bearish reading is that the global outlook has become dependent on a concentrated bet whose returns are not yet visible, and that a reversal would hit at a bad time. The IMF's downside scenario, in which AI-related investment unwinds, reduces global GDP by as much as 0.4% and investment by as much as 1.3% by 2028. That sounds modest, but it would coincide with the OECD's other identified risks, including renewed trade tensions and the energy shock, which together it reckons could subtract 0.7 percentage points from growth next year.

The public sector is poorly placed to cushion such a turn. The IMF's April Fiscal Monitor put global public debt at just under 94% of GDP in 2025, and IMF messaging at the October Annual Meetings in Bangkok warned it is on course to reach 100% of GDP by around the end of the decade; reports differ on whether that is 2029 or 2030. With headline inflation still above 4% globally, monetary policy also has less room than in 2020 or 2008.

Oil prices have offered some relief this month. Brent fell from above $100 at the start of November to the low-to-mid $90s by mid-month, according to market reports, on hopes of de-escalation and the IEA's projection that the market returns to surplus in the fourth quarter. If that holds, the energy drag on 2027 growth should fade, leaving AI investment to do less of the heavy lifting.

The upshot is a global economy that is more resilient than feared but less diversified than it looks. The key indicators to watch into 2027 are not only GDP prints but hyperscaler capex guidance in the coming earnings rounds, private credit spreads and redemptions, and whether data-centre utilisation and AI revenues begin to justify the build-out. The OECD's next full Economic Outlook, due in early December, will be the first major forecast to incorporate November's oil price retreat.
pieces.methodology: We compared the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook and April 2026 Fiscal Monitor, the OECD's June 2026 Economic Outlook and September 2026 interim report, and BIS publications from January and March 2026, alongside press coverage of company capex guidance and oil markets. pieces.headline: No Way Back: What the IEA's Hormuz Outlook Says About the Next Decade of Energy
pieces.dek: The International Energy Agency's 2026 World Energy Outlook treats this year's Gulf disruption as a structural break that will accelerate electrification and supply diversification, but the speed of change depends on how long the risk lingers.
key_findings: Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz fell from about 20 million barrels a day to around 3 mb/d between March and May 2026, which the IEA calls the largest energy supply shock the world has faced.
In a prolonged-risk case, bypass pipelines, alternative supply and demand displacement could cut the world's need for Hormuz oil to 8.5 mb/d by 2030 and below 2 mb/d by 2035.
Electricity's share of final energy consumption approaches 30% by 2035 in all of the IEA's exploratory scenarios, up from about 23% today.

Global energy investment is set to reach about $3.4 trillion in 2026, with roughly $2.2 trillion going to clean energy and grids against about $1.2 trillion for fossil fuels; oil upstream investment falls for a third year to below $500bn.
Under the Current Policies Scenario, energy-related CO2 emissions stay near today's level, underlining that security-driven change is not automatically climate-aligned.
body: Every November the IEA's World Energy Outlook sets the terms of the global energy debate. This year's edition, published on 19 November, opens with an unusually blunt judgement. The disruption to flows through the Strait of Hormuz in 2026, it says, has been the largest energy supply shock the world has faced and, as of November, it is not over. Fatih Birol, the agency's executive director, said he saw no 'credible pathway' for the energy world to return to the way it was before.

The physical numbers explain the language. According to the report, oil flows through the strait fell from roughly 20 mb/d to about 3 mb/d between March and May. The IEA's November Oil Market Report, cited in the outlook, puts the resulting decline in 2026 world oil demand at around 2.7 mb/d, demand destruction on a scale normally associated with deep recessions. Prices followed: Brent spent much of the year above $100 a barrel before easing into the $90s in November as Middle Eastern output recovered.

Rather than a single central forecast, the outlook is built around scenarios that vary by how long the threat to Gulf flows persists. The most striking is a prolonged-risk case in which governments and companies act to reduce exposure. Investment in bypass pipelines, alternative suppliers and demand displacement could reduce the world's need for oil to transit Hormuz from 20 mb/d to 8.5 mb/d by 2030 and to under 2 mb/d by 2035. In an extreme long-run disruption case, 2035 oil demand would be 4.4 mb/d below the Stated Policies Scenario, and the IEA says the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching accelerate.

The common thread across scenarios is electricity. The IEA projects electricity's share of final energy consumption approaching 30% by 2035 in all of its exploratory scenarios, from about 23% now, with demand already growing around 3.3% a year since 2019. Renewables grow faster than any other major source in every scenario, led by solar PV. Investment data back this up: the IEA's World Energy Investment 2026 report, published in May, projected total energy investment rising about 5% to $3.4 trillion this year, of which roughly $2.2 trillion goes to renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, efficiency and electrification and about $1.2 trillion to oil, gas and coal. Battery storage spending was expected to exceed $100bn, up more than 35%, while oil investment falls for a third consecutive year to below $500bn.

Gas is the most contested piece. The outlook says that in its Current Policies Scenario global gas demand still grows, but more slowly than in the Stated Policies case, and LNG demand takes a hit. That is a notable shift from last year's edition, which under current policies had LNG trade rising from about 560 bcm in 2024 to 880 bcm in 2035, partly on data-centre power demand. Importers that saw Gulf LNG cargoes disrupted are now weighing diversification against the risk of locking in another exposed supply chain.

Critics come from both directions. Some, such as the US-based Institute for Energy Research, which reviewed the report critically, argue that the IEA consistently understates the durability of oil and gas demand and that security concerns will drive more domestic fossil production, not less. Climate analysts counter that the Current Policies Scenario, in which only laws already on the books are implemented, leaves energy-related CO2 emissions roughly flat at today's level, far from any Paris-aligned path. Security-driven change, in other words, does not automatically mean decarbonisation; it can just as easily mean more coal in import-dependent Asia or more domestic oil elsewhere.

There is also a timing question. Oil markets are already pricing relief: the IEA's own November market report points to a significant production recovery and a return to surplus in the fourth quarter. If tensions ease and flows normalise, the political urgency behind diversification could fade, as it did after the 1970s shocks in some countries and not in others. The IEA's framing, that the duration of the shock will determine the scale of the change, is effectively an admission that policy, not geology, now drives the forecast.

The release came days after COP31 in Antalya, the largest climate conference on record by attendance, where the energy-security framing loomed over negotiations. The WEO gives both camps material: evidence that electrification is the most robust hedge against supply shocks, and evidence that without new policy, the system's emissions trajectory barely bends.

For governments and investors the practical takeaways are threefold. Grids and storage are now the binding constraint across all scenarios; the pace of supply-chain diversification for oil, LNG and clean-tech components will shape costs; and the gap between security-led and climate-led policy needs to be closed deliberately rather than assumed away.
pieces.methodology: We drew on the IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026 (executive summary, scenario chapters and press release), the IEA's World Energy Investment 2026 report, and the November 2026 Oil Market Report as cited in the WEO, supplemented by trade-press and analytical coverage. We were unable to read the full WEO text directly; some figures (such as the 4.4 mb/d extreme-case gap and the 3.3% annual electricity demand growth) are drawn from secondary summaries of the report. LNG trade projections cited are from the 2025 WEO for comparison and are not directly comparable with 2026 scenarios. A third-party estimate of cumulative supply lost was not verifiable and was excluded. We could not confirm the final outcome of COP31.

pieces.headline: The Great Retreat: Global Health Aid Falls to Its Lowest Level Since 2012
pieces.dek: As World AIDS Day approaches, new estimates show donor funding for health in poorer countries shrinking for a second year, with the burden shifting to multilateral banks, philanthropy and stretched domestic budgets.
key_findings: IHME's preliminary estimates put development assistance for health at $42.6bn in 2026, the lowest since 2012, after a further fall of about 5% following a steeper drop in 2025.
The UK made the largest absolute cut in 2026, reducing health aid by 37% ($891m); the US cut by 8% ($668m), and Canada and Germany by more than $100m each.
Disbursements by UN agencies fell an estimated 18% ($873m) and by Gavi 15% ($447m), while regional development banks rose 32% ($270m) and the Gates Foundation 4%.
The OECD projects ODA for health will fall 29-46% between 2024 and 2026, to its lowest level in almost two decades.

UNAIDS reports 1.2 million new HIV infections and 570,000 AIDS-related deaths in 2025, near 30-year lows, but warns that prevention funding cuts could push new infections up to 1.4 million a year by 2030.
body: For two decades, international health aid was one of the most reliable growth stories in development finance, peaking during the pandemic. That era is over. Preliminary estimates from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), summarised in October by the Council on Foreign Relations' Think Global Health, put development assistance for health at $42.6bn in 2026, its lowest level since 2012. The decline this year, of about 5%, is smaller than the collapse of 2025, but it is a second consecutive fall from an already reduced base.

The donor picture has shifted markedly. In 2026 the largest absolute cut came not from Washington but from London: IHME estimates the UK reduced its health aid by 37%, or $891m, as it redirected its aid budget. The US, after the dismantling of USAID in 2025, cut a further $668m, or 8%. Canada and Germany each reduced funding by more than $100m. Among major governments, Japan was a rare riser, up 2% ($32m). The OECD's own projections, using a different measure, are bleaker still: bilateral ODA for health is projected to fall by 29-46% between 2024 and 2026, to its lowest level in almost two decades.

The pain is transmitted through the multilateral system. IHME estimates that disbursements by UN agencies fell by 18% ($873m) and by Gavi, the vaccine alliance, by 15% ($447m) between 2025 and 2026. Sub-Saharan Africa, historically the largest recipient, has absorbed the biggest reduction relative to other regions. There are partial offsets: regional development banks increased health financing by an estimated 32% ($270m), and the Gates Foundation, now the second-largest single source behind the US, rose 4%. But neither is large enough to fill the gap left by bilateral donors.

HIV is the clearest test case of what the cuts mean in practice. UNAIDS data show 1.2 million new infections and 570,000 AIDS-related deaths in 2025, the lowest in more than 30 years. Yet the agency's July special report described the response as 'extremely fragile' and said prevention, which received only 11% of HIV funding in 2024, had been hit hardest. If current funding levels persist, UNAIDS projects new infections could rise to as many as 1.4 million a year by 2030. Conversely, the political declaration adopted by 149 member states in June could avert 3.2 million infections and 1.3 million deaths by 2030 if fully implemented. UNAIDS had flagged a Global AIDS Update for November ahead of World AIDS Day on 1 December.

The interpretive debate is real. One school argues the retrenchment is a long-overdue correction: donor-driven 'vertical' programmes created parallel systems, crowded out domestic investment and left countries dependent on foreign priorities. On this view, the rise of regional development banks and calls for countries to finance their own health systems signal a healthier, more sovereign model. Proponents point to middle-income countries that have taken over HIV treatment costs as evidence that transition is feasible.

The other school notes that the transition is happening by default rather than design, and at a moment when many recipient countries have the least fiscal room. The IMF projects global public debt approaching 100% of GDP by the end of the decade, and many low-income countries spend more on debt service than on health. This year's energy shock has added to import bills and inflation. Asking governments to absorb abrupt cuts to commodities such as antiretrovirals, vaccines and malaria nets risks interruptions whose costs, in drug resistance and resurgent transmission, appear only with a lag.

There are also measurement uncertainties. The 2026 IHME figures are preliminary and may be revised. Different data series produce different totals: one widely cited analysis of IHME data describes a fall of roughly half from an $80bn peak in 2021 to around $39bn, while the $42.6bn figure reflects a different vintage or definition. And aid data capture disbursements, not health outcomes; the epidemiological consequences of cuts in 2025-26 will take years to show up in mortality and infection statistics.

What is clear is the direction of travel. Health aid is now smaller, more concentrated in philanthropy and development banks, and less reliable year to year. The question for 2027 is whether the multilateral system, Gavi's and the Global Fund's next replenishment cycles, and recipient governments' budgets can adapt fast enough to protect the programmes, especially prevention, where gains are easiest to lose.

World AIDS Day next week will put the HIV numbers in the spotlight, but the same arithmetic applies to immunisation, maternal health and malaria. The evidence suggests the world is running an unplanned experiment in how quickly global health gains can be sustained without the funding that built them.
pieces.methodology: We examined IHME's preliminary Financing Global Health estimates for 2026 as reported by Think Global Health and the Ghana News Agency, OECD 2026 ODA projections for health, UNAIDS reports and press releases from June and July 2026, and IMF fiscal data. IHME's 2026 figures are preliminary and differ from other series; we note one conflicting total from secondary reporting. We could not confirm whether UNAIDS's planned November 2026 Global AIDS Update had been published at the time of writing. Aid flows measure inputs, not health outcomes, and attribution of future infection or mortality changes to funding cuts involves modelling assumptions.

items.title: Why oil is climbing again, and what OPEC+ does next
items.dek: Attacks on Gulf shipping and Saudi refineries have pulled Brent off a three-month low just before producers meet on 2027 output, but the bigger picture still points to a glut.

slides.title: Brent snaps a four-week losing streak
slides.text: Brent crude traded near $96.60 a barrel early on Friday, heading for a weekly rise of about 4% and its first weekly gain in four weeks. Only days earlier, worries about oversupply had pushed it to a three-month low. The trigger for the turnaround was a run of attacks on tankers and energy facilities in the Gulf.

visual.label: Brent crude per barrel, 27 Nov (04:50 GMT)
visual.sub: On course for a weekly gain of about 4%, after trading near $89 on 24 Nov

slides.title: The strait that broke the oil market
slides.text: The International Energy Agency calls this year's disruption at the Strait of Hormuz the largest energy supply shock the world has faced. Flows through the strait fell from about 20 million barrels a day to around 3 mb/d between March and May, and the IEA estimates world oil demand fell by about 2.7 mb/d in 2026. In a prolonged-risk case, bypass pipelines, other suppliers and lower demand could shrink the world's need for Hormuz oil sharply over the next decade.

slides.title: Five days of escalation
slides.text: The week's attacks hit both sides of the supply chain: shipping lanes and refineries. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said tankers moving through Hormuz without its permission had struck sea mines, claims that could not be independently verified, while the US said it was continuing to enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports. Yemen's Houthis, aligned with Iran, targeted Saudi refineries.

slides.title: Rerouting is costly
slides.text: The risk premium reflects real costs to trade as well as fears over supply. Container line Hapag-Lloyd estimates that sending ships around the strait costs it more than EUR 60 million a week. Iran says the waterway is closed to unauthorised traffic, and the US Treasury has added sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and officials.

slides.text: Analysts disagree about which force will win. Supply risks in the Gulf argue for higher prices, while inventories and demand data point the other way. Both camps agree that Sunday's OPEC+ decision and events at Hormuz will set the direction.

items.title: Wall Street's whiplash week, explained
items.dek: A restored Nvidia chief, an intraday rout and a looming Fed hike sent stocks on a round trip before Friday's half-day session, and the AI trade is still at the centre of it.

slides.title: Buyers come back for a half-day
slides.text: US stock futures rose sharply before Friday's shortened Black Friday session, which ends at 1pm ET. Early on Friday, Nasdaq 100 futures were up close to 3%, S&P 500 futures about 1.7% and Dow futures about 1%. The buying was concentrated in the artificial-intelligence and chip stocks that had been hit hardest this month.

visual.label: Gain in Nasdaq 100 futures early Friday
visual.sub: S&P 500 futures up about 1.7%, Dow futures about 1%; NYSE and Nasdaq close at 1pm ET

slides.title: A round trip in five sessions
slides.text: The week began with a surge in Nvidia and ended with a rebound, but the days in between were rough. On Wednesday the S&P 500 fell as much as 3.2% intraday before recovering most of the loss. Even so, AP figures had the S&P up about 3.9% for the week through Wednesday.

slides.title: The rebound travelled, unevenly
slides.text: Once Wall Street stepped away for the holiday, Europe and then Asia rallied on technology stocks. India was the exception: the Sensex fell 1.17% as Brent topped $97 a barrel, hurting an oil-importing economy. Note that the closes below fall on different days because markets kept different holiday hours.

slides.title: It's all about AI
slides.text: Nvidia's 31% jump on Huang's return lifted the whole market, but the gains faded as doubts returned over whether customers borrowing heavily to build data centres will earn back their spending. Reports said Nvidia had lost more than $2 trillion in market value from its October peak. Results were mixed: Analog Devices slumped, while Dell posted $22 billion of AI-server revenue and raised its full-year guidance.

slides.title: A Fed hike is all but certain
slides.text: October PCE inflation reached 3.8%, with core at 3.3%, and traders now treat a quarter-point Fed rate rise at the 8-9 December meeting as all but certain. Polymarket put the odds at 93.5% on 25 November, and some Fed officials have floated larger or additional moves. Treasury yields have eased nonetheless, with the 10-year near 4.86% after topping 5% earlier in the month.

items.title: Separate Cheques
items.caption: Two schools of thought at the Grid Café: close the kitchen, or ask for separate cheques.
items.alt: At a café table under a sign reading Grid Café, a small, startled Everyman in a bowler hat sits with a tiny cup of tea while a very long bill marked kWh unrolls off the table to the floor in front of him. Across the table a big, cheerful robot built like a server rack, wearing a napkin bib and plugged into the wall socket, tucks into a heaped plate of lightning bolts. Behind the table two identical suited officials hold up placards: one reads Close the Kitchen!, the other Separate Cheques!
items.story: This week's opinion debate asks whether states should pause new AI data-centre construction until rules protect ratepayers, or keep building and make data centres pay their own grid costs.

items.title: The Hormuz Tiptoe
items.caption: Out at sea, everyone tiptoes. Ashore, the boldest plan on the table is ‘same again’.
items.alt: A nervous oil tanker labelled Crude, its bridge windows drawn as wide worried eyes, wades on tiptoe on four spindly legs through a sea dotted with bobbing spiked sea mines, sweat drops flying. A signpost in the water reads Brent $95 with an upward arrow. On a headland, under a pavilion marked OPEC+ Meeting, three small suited ministers sit at a table; a speech bubble says Bold proposal: same again, and another replies Hear, hear!
items.story: Oil rallied to the mid-$90s this week after reported mine strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on Saudi refineries, with OPEC+ ministers meeting on Sunday and expected to roll over current output targets.

lex.intro: Lex weighs where the money could be made next in India, the United States, Europe and the developing world: the argument, the numbers behind it, and the case against.

regions.summary: Indian equities have de-rated to a forward P/E of roughly 17-18x, below the long-period average of about 21x (MOFSL, BofA), even as Nifty profits grew about 25% in the September quarter (Elara). Foreign money came back in November, but CPI inflation of 6.09% and an RBI that has started raising rates mean the cheap money behind the last re-rating is gone.

notes.title: Lenders at a discount, on a rising tide
notes.examples: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, State Bank of India; or a Nifty Bank index fund
body: The Nifty Bank index hit a record intraday high of 62,324.55 on 17 November (Free Press Journal), helped by foreign buying. The rally is better grounded than the headline suggests. RBI data reported by Angel One show system credit growth of 19.26% in the fortnight to 31 October, up from 17.94% the fortnight before. Elara puts Nifty 50 profit growth for Q2 FY27 at 24.7%, with financials a large part of it.

Valuation is the attraction. Jefferies said in late September that HDFC Bank trades at a 26% discount to ICICI Bank on price-to-book, up from 11% in March (Business Today). The largest franchise in the country priced as a laggard is the kind of gap that tends to close when loan growth comes back, and it is coming back.

The rate cycle cuts both ways. The RBI's 25bp hike to 5.5% in October (Moneylife) supports yields on floating-rate loan books, but it also raises deposit costs at a time when credit is growing 2.5 percentage points faster than deposits. Lex prefers the large, deposit-rich incumbents to faster-growing mid-sized lenders, whose valuation premium brokers say has widened.
bull: Credit growth is running near 19% a year, the fastest in years (RBI data via Angel One)
HDFC Bank's 26% price-to-book discount to ICICI Bank leaves room for a re-rating (Jefferies via Business Today)
Foreign investors are rotating out of crowded US AI trades and back into Indian financials
bear: Inflation of 6.09% in October breached the RBI's 6% ceiling, so a further hike at the 2-4 December meeting is possible; higher rates usually push up bad loans with a lag
Loans are growing faster than deposits, which squeezes funding costs; HDFC Bank's margin fell 9bp year on year to 3.26% in Q1 FY27 (S&P Global)
After a roughly 13% gain in November, a large part of the good news may already be priced in

notes.title: Wires before watts
notes.examples: Power Grid Corporation of India, Hitachi Energy India, GE Vernova T&D India
body: India is adding renewable capacity faster than it can move the power. A report cited by Open magazine puts planned transmission capex at about Rs9 trillion by 2032. Power Grid alone has guided to an initial Rs37,000 crore of capex for FY27 (T&D India). Transmission projects run on regulated returns and decade-long build cycles, which makes them about as close to a contracted growth story as Indian equities offer.

The equipment makers are where the operating leverage sits. Transformer, HVDC and switchgear suppliers are working through record order books, and the bottleneck is factory capacity, not demand. That gives suppliers pricing power for as long as utilities are queuing for kit.

Lex's caution is about price. Business Standard has flagged that Power Grid's valuations remain elevated despite a strong outlook, and the listed equipment makers trade at multiples that assume flawless execution. Buyers should treat the theme as a holding to accumulate on dips, not a trade to chase.

Regulated returns at Power Grid make the cash flows bond-like
Equipment suppliers have pricing power while capacity is short
bear: Valuations are already elevated, which leaves little margin for error (Business Standard)

notes.title: Defence: right story, wrong price
notes.examples: Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL), Bharat Electronics (BEL); or a Nifty India Defence index fund
body: The case for Indian defence stocks is not in dispute. The defence ministry is reportedly seeking a 20% increase in capital spending (Kotak Neo), and import substitution steers that money to domestic suppliers. BEL's order book stood at Rs68,717 crore after a fresh Rs619 crore win in mid-November (Kotak Neo). HAL's order book is put at about Rs2.5 trillion.

The trouble is that the market got there first. A Nuvama note in March put the Nifty Defence index at about 52 times earnings and BEL near 50 times, with HAL the relative bargain at about 28 times (Whalesbook). Those are growth-stock multiples for state-owned companies whose revenue depends on one customer's procurement timetable.

Execution is the weak link. HAL posted a record order book alongside revenue growth of only about 7% (The Core), which shows how slowly orders turn into deliveries. Lex would own the theme, with HAL the least stretched name, but would wait for a pullback rather than pay today's prices.
bull: A rising capex budget and indigenisation rules give multi-year demand visibility
Order books worth several years of revenue at HAL and BEL
Export ambitions add an upside option beyond the domestic budget
bear: Index valuation of about 52x earnings leaves no room for disappointment (Nuvama via Whalesbook)
Orders are slow to convert into revenue: HAL grew revenue only about 7% despite a record backlog (The Core)
Single-customer risk: budget delays or reallocations hit everyone at once

regions.summary: US earnings are growing at about 33% in 2026 (FactSet), so the S&P 500's forward P/E has fallen to about 18x, below its 5-year average, even with the index near record highs. The risk has moved to rates: the Fed raised rates in September, markets expect another hike in December, and the 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%.

notes.title: AI's sell-off has outrun its earnings
notes.examples: Nvidia, Broadcom; or a broad semiconductor index fund
body: AI stocks have had a bruising autumn. One tally of 49 AI and AI-infrastructure stocks found the median 40.7% below its all-time high, with 13 down by at least half (Finviz). Over the same period, the numbers have gone the other way. Nvidia's third-quarter revenue was $115.8bn, up 103%, data-centre revenue was $107.6bn, up 110%, and it guided to $130bn for the current quarter.

The result is a market where the leaders' earnings have run ahead of their share prices. FactSet notes that the S&P 500's forward P/E fell to 17.7 in early November, its lowest since late 2023, because forward earnings estimates rose 33.6% year to date while the index rose just 7.4%. In a market priced like that, owning the companies doing the earning is reasonable.

Lex prefers the picks-and-shovels suppliers with cash profits today to the borrowers building the capacity. Hyperscalers are increasingly paying for the build-out with debt rather than cash on hand (BNN Bloomberg). If that funding gets more expensive, orders slow, and the suppliers find out last.
bull: Revenue is still roughly doubling: Nvidia revenue rose 103% y/y and it guided to $130bn for next quarter
The sell-off has compressed valuations while earnings forecasts kept rising (FactSet)
Capacity due in 2027 is largely already under construction, which supports near-term orders
bear: Capex is increasingly funded with debt, so a 10-year yield near 5% is a direct threat to the build-out
The new Democratic-controlled Congress could step up scrutiny of AI and Big Tech
Concentration risk: about 93% of Nvidia's revenue comes from data centres, and large customers can cut orders quickly

notes.title: The grid is the real bottleneck
notes.theme: Power equipment and utilities serving data-centre demand
notes.examples: GE Vernova, Constellation Energy, Southern Co; or a utilities sector index fund
body: However the chip cycle turns out, every data centre needs power, and the US grid was not built for this load. Morningstar expects US data-centre electricity demand to roughly triple between 2024 and 2030. Turbines, transformers and switchgear are booked years ahead. GE Vernova's backlog rose by $20bn in a single quarter to $197bn, and its electrification equipment backlog grew 60% to $42.2bn (Zacks).

This is the safer way to own the AI build-out. Equipment makers are paid upfront and through reservation fees, and utilities earn regulated returns on the poles and wires. Morningstar's Q3 report rates the utilities sector roughly fairly valued, with earnings expected to grow 6-8% a year, which is respectable for a sector that pays dividends.

The catch is that the market noticed some time ago. Utilities had risen about a third over 12 months in Morningstar's earlier analysis, and equipment makers trade on demand forecasts that hyperscalers have yet to sign for in full. With the 10-year Treasury near 5%, bond-like utilities face real competition from bonds themselves.

GE Vernova has a $197bn backlog and expects it to pass $200bn in Q4 (Zacks)
Utilities look fairly valued with 6-8% earnings growth (Morningstar)
bear: A 10-year Treasury yield near 5% makes regulated, dividend-paying utilities less attractive
If AI capex slows, the demand forecasts these stocks are priced on go with it; Morningstar names data-centre demand uncertainty as the sector's main risk

notes.title: Healthcare's haven is now fully priced
notes.examples: Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie; or a healthcare sector index fund
body: Healthcare has been the refuge for investors leaving tech in 2026. Reuters reported the S&P 500 healthcare sector up more than 19% this year to record highs, behind only energy. Eli Lilly hit an intraday record of $1,307.91 on 20 October (Grafa) on demand for its GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. A sector with steady earnings and real innovation is a reasonable thing to own when rates are rising.

The trouble is that the price now assumes the good news. Longbridge puts the sector's forward P/E at 19.7, which it says makes healthcare the most expensive sector relative to its own 5-year average. A sector that was once a value play now trades above the S&P 500's roughly 18x forward multiple (FactSet).

Politics adds a further risk. Democrats took both chambers of Congress in November, and strategists warned that a Democratic sweep could build momentum behind measures on drug prices and healthcare costs. Lex likes the franchises but would wait for a policy scare to buy them more cheaply.

A Democratic Congress raises the risk of tougher drug-pricing legislation and scrutiny of insurers

regions.summary: Europe is pricing an energy-driven inflation shock: euro area inflation hit 4.0% in October, the ECB has raised rates twice this year and economists expect a third rise to 2.75% in December, while the Bank of England raised its rate to 4% in November. Stocks still trade at a hefty discount to Wall Street, so the opportunity lies in sectors that gain from higher rates and bigger budgets, or that have already been marked down, not in the index as a whole.

notes.title: Rheinmetall: the sell-off has gone further than the problems
notes.theme: European defence after the November rout
body: On 5 November Rheinmetall lowered its 2026 sales forecast to about EUR13.2bn, down from EUR13.7bn-14.2bn, blaming slow contract signings and delayed ammunition acceptance tests. Reuters reported the shares fell 16% that day. By 11 November they were about 49% below their 2025 close. When Germany cancelled the F126 frigate, the selling spread to Hensoldt and Renk.

The numbers underneath have held up better than the share price. Nine-month sales rose 38% to EUR8.4bn, operating profit was a record EUR1.34bn, and the backlog grew to EUR78bn from EUR56.7bn a year earlier. Fixed orders now make up 70% of it, against 58%. Berlin's 2027 budget lifts core defence spending to about EUR109bn from about EUR82bn, and the finance ministry has defence rising to 3.5% of GDP by 2029.

What went wrong is timing: contracts are signing later than promised, while demand is unchanged. Investors who paid for perfect execution have been punished, and a backlog that keeps growing while the price halves is the kind of mismatch Lex looks for. Our preference is to buy in instalments rather than all at once, because more guidance slips are possible before the Arminius contract signs, now expected in Q1 2027.
bull: Backlog of EUR78bn is about six times the cut 2026 sales guidance, and a larger share of it is now firm orders
German core defence spending is set to rise by roughly a third in 2027, and the debt-brake exemption for defence means the money is not at the mercy of annual fiscal fights
A halved share price means a lot of bad news has already been absorbed
bear: Getting things done is the problem: further delays to programmes or acceptance tests would push revenue further out, and the EUR100bn year-end backlog target now looks out of reach
Progress in Ukraine peace talks has repeatedly knocked the sector, and a ceasefire could reduce urgency even if the structural spending plans stay
Cancelled programmes such as the F126 show that a bigger budget still does not guarantee orders for any one listed name

notes.title: European banks: higher rates help, but the cheap shares are gone
notes.theme: Eurozone and UK banks in a re-tightening cycle
notes.examples: BNP Paribas (BNP.PA), Banco Santander (SAN.MC), Deutsche Bank (DBK.DE)
body: Few sectors gain from an inflation shock, and banks are one of them. The ECB has raised its deposit rate to 2.50%, and economists in a Reuters poll taken 10-12 November expect 2.75% in December. Third-quarter results bore this out: Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas and Santander all beat forecasts. BNP's profit rose 14% to EUR3.46bn, with volatile markets lifting equities trading.

The trouble is that investors already know this. Over the two years to October 2026 the Stoxx 600 Banks index rose 85.6%, against 25.8% for the wider Stoxx 600. In May the ECB's own Financial Stability Review said euro area bank valuations had reached levels last seen before the financial crisis, and asked whether they could last. HSBC's shares fell more than 5% after its results, a sign of how little room there is for disappointment.

The case still stands on yield and payouts: a LSEG-based comparison puts European banks at about 1.17 times book, against 1.7 times for US rivals. But the cheap re-rating has happened. Profits should keep climbing on higher net interest income while bad loans stay low; another doubling of the shares should not be expected.
bull: One more ECB hike is widely expected, and markets price further tightening, which supports net interest margins
Q3 beats at BNP, Deutsche and Santander show profits still rising, with trading income an added boost in volatile markets
Still at a discount to US banks on price-to-book, and buybacks remain generous (UBS accelerated its buyback)
bear: The ECB says valuations are at pre-crisis highs, so with expectations this high any miss gets punished, as HSBC found
An energy-led recession would bring loan losses; Santander's results were already hurt by higher provisions in Brazil
If energy prices collapse, the rate-hike story unwinds quickly and Deutsche Bank sees December as the last hike

notes.title: FTSE 100: cheap, unloved, and built for a world of costly energy
notes.theme: UK large caps as a value and inflation hedge
notes.examples: iShares Core FTSE 100 UCITS ETF (ISF); Shell (SHEL.L), HSBC (HSBA.L)
body: London's blue-chip index trades on about 12.1 times forward earnings, cheaper than the FTSE 250 at 13.4 times, according to a 4 November Saxo outlook. A Reuters poll in August put the whole Stoxx 600 at about 14.6 times, a 26% discount to US shares. The FTSE 100 is cheaper still, mainly because it is weighted to oil, mining, banks and consumer staples rather than technology.

This year that mix has worked in its favour. The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% on 4 November by an 8-1 vote, with one member wanting a half-point rise. It now expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027 as energy costs feed through. An index heavy in energy producers and banks is one of the few in the developed world that gains when oil stays high and rates rise.

Saxo argues the low multiple reflects what the index is made of, not better-quality earnings, and it is right that this is no growth story. For a patient holder, though, the cheap starting valuation plus large dividends and buybacks have historically done much of the work, and London is a natural counterweight to a US-heavy portfolio.
bull: About 12 times forward earnings, a large discount to the US and to its own mid-cap index
Heavy weighting in energy, miners and banks hedges the oil-and-rates shock driving 2026
Most FTSE 100 earnings come from abroad, so a weaker pound tends to lift sterling profits
bear: Little technology exposure means the index lags badly whenever AI-led growth stocks rally
If the Middle East conflict ends and oil collapses, the energy hedge turns into a drag

notes.title: Vietnam: the market has been upgraded, foreign investors are still selling
notes.theme: Vietnam after the FTSE Russell emerging-market upgrade
notes.examples: VanEck Vietnam ETF (VNM); Vietcombank (VCB), FPT Corp (FPT)
body: FTSE Russell's move of Vietnam from frontier to emerging status took effect on 21 September. Estimates of the passive money it would attract ranged from $1.2bn (HSBC) to FTSE's own scenario of $3bn-9bn. Instead, a FireAnt-sourced tracker shows foreign investors were net sellers in 31 of the 34 sessions after the upgrade, taking out about VND29.7trn. The VN-Index fell 3.5% in September and 1.6% in October, and foreigners dumped bank shares again in early November.

The economy has not slowed. Vietnam grew 7.8% year on year in Q1, 8.4% in Q2 and a reported 9.95% in Q3, beating the 8.65% consensus. Hanoi is aiming for 10% for the year. Index inclusion is phased in over four tranches until September 2027, so most of the mechanical buying is still ahead.

Lex thinks this sell-the-news reaction is the opportunity. Selling by the same foreign funds that should eventually own the market has made a fast-growing economy cheaper. The caveat is forecasting: the OECD expects only 6.5% growth in 2026, and the gap between official numbers and sceptics is wide.
bull: GDP growth near 10% in Q3 is among the fastest of any sizeable economy
Three of four FTSE inclusion tranches remain to come, through September 2027, and an MSCI upgrade is the next prize
Weeks of foreign net selling since the upgrade have cleared out crowded positioning
bear: Liquidity and foreign ownership limits mean exits can be costly; bank shares, the index heavyweights, are where foreigners are selling
As a big exporter, Vietnam is exposed to US tariff policy and a strong dollar
Official growth figures may flatter: forecasts range from 6.5% (OECD) to 9.5% (Standard Chartered)

notes.title: Brazil: high real rates pay you to wait, but wait for the fiscal deal
notes.theme: Brazilian equities and the stalled Selic easing cycle
notes.examples: iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ); Itau Unibanco (ITUB), Petrobras (PBR)
body: On 4 November Brazil's central bank surprised markets by keeping the Selic at 13.75%, pausing the easing it began after holding at 15% from June 2025 to March 2026. The minutes were hawkish. Copom now projects inflation of 5.6% in 2026 and 4.7% in 2027, well above the 3% target, citing oil prices, El Niño, the end of the six-day working week and a weaker real.

Equities are trading on fiscal headlines. The Ibovespa hit a three-month low of 169,186 on 29 October as post-election doubts grew. It rallied to about 172,500 after Lula's team sent Congress a fiscal adjustment plan, then fell 1.8% to 169,295 on 16 November. The real lost 2.9% against the dollar in the week to 13 November, to R$5.67, even as the central bank recorded $1.3bn of foreign inflows.

With double-digit real policy rates, the eventual easing cycle could re-rate banks and domestic stocks sharply. But the trigger has to be a credible fiscal deal that brings inflation expectations back down, and the Senate has yet to deliver one. Until it does, Lex would collect the carry in fixed income and wait to buy equities.
bull: A Selic of 13.75% against inflation expectations of about 5% leaves real rates very high, giving plenty of room to cut later
Foreign dollar inflows continued even in a bad week for the real
Passage of the fiscal adjustment bill would be a clear catalyst for both the currency and domestic equities
bear: Fiscal credibility after Lula's re-election is unproven, and the bill may be watered down
Currency risk: a 2.9% weekly fall in the real wipes out a lot of carry for dollar-based investors
Bank asset quality is fraying: Santander blamed Brazil for higher provisions and Banco do Brasil disappointed in Q3

notes.title: Saudi Arabia: the market is now open, but the oil revenue is not arriving
notes.theme: Gulf diversification and Tadawul's opening to foreign investors
notes.examples: iShares MSCI Saudi Arabia ETF (KSA); Saudi Aramco (2222.SR), Al Rajhi Bank (1120.SR)
body: On 1 February Riyadh opened its main market to every category of foreign investor. In the second quarter foreigners put $1.6bn into the Tadawul, the only Gulf market where net foreign buying rose. The exchange's chief executive is targeting $100bn of foreign ownership by 2030. Lifting the remaining 49% foreign ownership cap on listed companies, which the regulator has promised, would raise Saudi Arabia's weight in MSCI's EM index.

The war, however, has interrupted the oil windfall. Aramco's Q3 net income rose 34.5% to $36.3bn, but the state's oil revenue fell by between 23% and almost 40% in the quarter depending on the measure, and the budget deficit was SAR84.3bn ($22.5bn). EnterpriseAM reports that the TASI fell 9.1% in November.

The structural story of market reform, deepening liquidity and Vision 2030 diversification is real. But the market's direction still depends on Hormuz and on government spending that now has to be funded with debt. Lex would wait for either the ownership-cap decision or a clearer end to the shipping disruption before buying.
bull: Full foreign access since February, with a pending 49% cap removal that would lift index weights and passive demand
Aramco profits are rising strongly, with Brent above $100 as recently as early October, and economists expect state oil revenue to rebound in Q4
A 9% fall in November makes the entry price better for patient money
bear: Hormuz disruption limits exports; Saudi Arabia is exposed to the same war that is lifting oil prices
Deficits are widening and the state is borrowing more, which may slow the Vision 2030 projects that drive domestic earnings
The 2025 Tadawul was its worst year in a decade, and foreign flows have proved fickle since the opening
